description: Solo participant, curious about fire in space and how real NASA data can help keep crews safe. Space Apps Salamanca.
summary:
Ember Guard is a small guardian robot that watches the air on a spacecraft when the crew cannot, and warns them before a fire can start.

Astronauts spend about a third of every mission asleep and most of the rest busy with demanding work. NASA schedules 8.5 hours of sleep on the ISS, yet crews average only about 6 (𝐵𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑟 𝑒𝑡 𝑎𝑙. 𝐿𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝑁𝑒𝑢𝑟𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑦, 2014). Rest is health in space, and no one rests well without knowing the air is safe.

Ember flies to a module, grips a handrail with its bottom gripper and switches its thrusters off so it does not disturb the airflow. An explainable AI model trained on 118 real ISS fire tests from NASA's BASS-II experiment turns its readings of oxygen and airflow into one clear answer: could this air keep a flame alive? Its live dashboard shows the risk and the reasons, and Ember can cut ventilation in that module as a preventive step.

𝐼𝑡 𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠 𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑘; 𝑖𝑡 𝑑𝑜𝑒𝑠 𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑑𝑒𝑡𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑠. 𝐸𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑟 𝑤𝑎𝑡𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑎𝑖𝑟, 𝑠𝑜 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑐𝑟𝑒𝑤 𝑐𝑎𝑛 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑡.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ember Guard is a small cabin robot that watches the air when the crew cannot: while they are busy with demanding work or unavailable, for example asleep. It flies to a module, grips a handrail with its bottom gripper and switches its thrusters off, so it does not disturb the airflow it is measuring. It reads oxygen, CO2, airflow, temperature and humidity, and estimates how likely that air is to sustain a flame, before any flame exists. If the risk is high, it warns the crew with eye colour, voice and sound, can cut ventilation in that module as a preventive step, and sends a report to the crew wherever they are.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: I transcribed every test in Appendix A of NASA's BASS-II summary report (122 ISS burn tests, 340 observed conditions), each row citing its page. 118 tests and 334 conditions are used by the model.

- Model: an explainable logistic regression with oxygen %, airflow (log scale plus a curve term, so it captures both "too little air" extinction and "too much wind" blowoff) and fuel type. The error band comes from 300 bootstrap fits.

- Validation: grouped cross-validation by test, so no experiment is used for both training and scoring. Held-out AUC 0.79; Brier score 0.150 versus 0.191 for a no-skill guess.

- Live dashboard: a single web page that works offline, with the robot's face, a real-time risk graph, a module map where the crew can cut ventilation with one click, "what if" sliders, saved reports, a scripted night shift, and a closed-domain voice and text chat that only answers air and fire-safety questions.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Rest is health in space: NASA schedules 8.5 hours of sleep on the ISS, yet crews average about 6. Fire is one of the most serious emergencies on a spacecraft, and flames in microgravity behave differently from flames on Earth. Ember Guard moves safety from reacting to a fire to preventing the conditions for one, keeps watch when no one can, and keeps astronauts away from a risky module until the risk is known. The crew always stays in charge.

CREATIVITY

Instead of another chart of past experiments, decades of microgravity combustion research become a character the crew can talk to and a single answer they can act on in seconds: could this air keep a flame alive right now? The robot, its gripper and its "thrusters off" behaviour are my own hand-drawn design.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about limits: it estimates risk, it does not detect or extinguish fires. It is valid only inside the tested ranges (O2 about 13.6-22.2 %, airflow 0.4-47 cm/s, about 1 atm, lab fuels such as PMMA and cotton-fiberglass). CO2, temperature and humidity are reported but are not model inputs, because BASS-II did not vary them. The dataset is small, so the model is for ranking risk, not for safety-critical decisions alone. The robot is a digital concept; no hardware was built.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, scikit-learn) for the dataset and model, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the dashboard, Web Speech API for the voice, three.js for the 3D views, Playwright and FFmpeg for the animated video, Tripo3D for the 3D model, Gemini for the music.

PATH FORWARD

Who could use it: commercial space stations replacing the ISS, lunar and Mars habitats, and long missions where the crew is small and help is far away. The first product would be software, not hardware: the risk model and live dashboard running on sensors a station already has, licensed to station operators. The robot is the second step, built with a space hardware partner. Every gram costs money to launch, so the robot would be made from lightweight, low-flammability materials suited to spacecraft cabins: a light shell that adds almost no mass, will not feed a fire itself and protects the crew with its soft bumper. The same idea also fits closed places on Earth where people sleep or work without watching the air, such as submarines, polar research stations and offshore platforms, if the model is retrained with data for those conditions.
